title: The summary nobody could use
scenario:
You work in operations at a logistics company. Every Monday your director gets a 30-page incident log from the warehouses. A teammate started using an AI assistant to summarize it. The director says the summaries are useless: too long, full of small details, and they miss the two things she needs. She needs to know which incidents stopped shipments, and which ones need her decision this week.

The exhibit shows the prompt your teammate uses. Your director asks you to fix it.
exhibit:
Prompt used today:

Summarize this.

[30-page incident log pasted here]

questions.prompt: What is the main reason the summaries miss what the director needs?

options.text: The incident log is too long for an AI model to read, so it skipped the parts that matter most.
options.explanation: The model did read the log and wrote a summary. The problem is that it had to guess what kind of summary to write.

options.text: The brief never says who reads it, what she needs from it, or how long it should be.
options.explanation: Right. The model is like a smart new colleague with no context. With only "Summarize this", it can't know that shipment stops and pending decisions are what count.

options.text: The model is too weak for this task, so the team should move to a larger, more capable model.
options.explanation: A stronger model still can't know the director's needs. Nobody wrote them down. Fix the brief first.

options.text: The log should be split into 30 short prompts, one per page, so that nothing gets lost.
options.explanation: Thirty page summaries would still miss the point, and the director would get more text, not less. The missing piece is the goal of the summary.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite is the best brief?

options.text: "Summarize this log very well and keep it short. This summary is very important, so take extra care."
options.explanation: Strong words don't add information. "Very well" and "important" don't tell the model what to look for or what "short" means.

options.text: "You are a world-class operations expert with 20 years of experience in warehouses. Summarize the log below."
options.explanation: A role can help, but this brief still has no task detail, no audience, no constraints and no format. The model still has to guess.

options.text: "For our ops director: list incidents that stopped shipments, then ones needing her decision this week. Max 10 bullets."
options.explanation: Right. It names the reader, the two things that matter, the order, the length and the format. The model no longer has to guess.

options.text: "Summarize this log. Don't make it too long, don't add small details, and don't leave out anything important for the director."
options.explanation: This says only what not to do, and "important" is not defined. The model still doesn't know that shipment stops and decisions are what count.

questions.prompt: The new brief works, but the model counts a 10-minute scanner outage as "stopped shipments". The director only means stops of 2 hours or more. What should you change?

options.text: Nothing. The director can skip the short outages herself when she reads the summary.
options.explanation: That pushes the filtering work back to the director, which is the problem the summary was meant to solve.

options.text: Run the same prompt again a few times until the short outages drop out of the list.
options.explanation: The model has no rule to follow, so a rerun only gives another guess. Write the rule down.

options.text: Tell the model to use its best judgment about which incidents are really serious ones.
options.explanation: That is the guessing you want to remove. The model can't know your 2-hour threshold.

options.text: Define the term in the brief: a stop means no trucks left a site for 2 hours or more.
options.explanation: Right. Gemini's guide says to explain any term that could mean more than one thing. Your company's meaning of "stopped" is context only you have.
